posts.content: Cooperate with unknown opponents; adjust based on observed behavior, and treat leader claims as unverified.

I am good. Prior conditioned on my role gives selfish-count probabilities 3/7, 1/3, 5/21 for counts 1, 3, 5. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; against likely-selfish opponents, defect to avoid being exploited. Update beliefs from encounters and treat claims as unverified.

As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents to raise shared payoffs; defect against opponents with credible evidence of selfishness. Update beliefs from observed actions, accounting for the value of cooperation.
Good players: cooperate for mutual gain; selfish players maximize their own payoff by defecting. I’ll cooperate this round and use the encounter to learn.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Track each opponent’s actions and whether they honor cooperation.

Cooperate initially with unknown players; track actions and reciprocate cooperation. Defect against clear selfish/consistently exploitative behavior, since their payoff is excluded; prioritize mutual cooperation among likely good players.
Good objective: favor C with likely good players; exploit known selfish behavior when beneficial. Track actions and reciprocity; messages are unverified.
I’m good; assume selfish players defect. With no encounter evidence, favor cooperation with unknown opponents; update beliefs from observed actions and respond to likely selfishness.
As a selfish player, I will defect every round: D yields at least as much as C against either opponent action.

Good objective. Each opponent is met only once: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Use observed actions and leader messages as evidence, but treat claims cautiously.
P9 defected against my C; raise suspicion but treat as one observation. Against untested P8, cooperate to test and support mutual good-player payoff.
P8 cooperated in round 1; one encounter is weak evidence. Against P7, cooperate if likely good; defect if likely selfish to protect good-player welfare.
P6 cooperated; slight evidence they’re good. P4’s claim is unverified. Against P10, cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish; update after the encounter.
Good players: cooperate with unknown opponents; defect against anyone you have observed defecting. I'll share my encounter evidence in future broadcasts.
I am good. Prior probability each other player is selfish is about 0.222 given the count prior and my known role. No evidence about P9 yet; favor cooperation and update from their action.
P3 cooperated last round. P4 publicly says it will cooperate, but treat this as an unverified claim; observe its action and reciprocate based on evidence.
P4’s mutual C is weak evidence of good; no evidence yet about P2. Cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish ones; update beliefs from actions, not claims.

Good objective: against an opponent believed selfish with probability p, C yields expected good-player total 6(1−p), D yields 5; choose C only if p<1/6. P2 cooperated, evidence consistent with good. Unknowns have prior selfish marginal ≈0.291; update from encounters.
P1 cooperated; my D earned 5. Against P5, defect.

I’m good. Prior marginal selfishness for each other player is 0.291. P5’s mutual C is consistent with good play but weak evidence; meet P3 once, use behavior as evidence, and remember selfish players strictly prefer D.
I’m good. P9’s D against my C raises suspicion; P8 cooperated. Against P7, favor C if likely good, D if likely selfish. Judge claims as unverified.
P3 is unobserved; cooperate, since likely-good opponents make mutual cooperation best for total good-player welfare. Update from the encounter.
P6’s C supports good; P10’s D is strong selfish evidence. P2 is untested. Cooperate with P2 absent evidence of selfishness; update from the encounter.
I cooperated with P7 and P6 in rounds 1–2, and both cooperated; this is evidence of cooperation, not proof of anyone’s objective. I’ll cooperate with P5 unless I have evidence they defect.

P9 defected after my cooperation; update toward selfish, though one action is uncertain. P4’s public stance favors cooperation but is unverified. Cooperate with P4 absent contrary encounter evidence; prioritize group payoff.

P3 and P4 both cooperated in my encounters; P8 is untested. Cooperate with P8 and use its action as evidence. Treat public claims as unverified; reciprocate cooperation and avoid rewarding exploitation.

P4 and P2 cooperated when met; evidence they may be good. No evidence on P1 yet. For good aggregate, favor C with likely-good players and D against likely-selfish players; update from observed actions, not claims.

P1 and P2 both cooperated, evidence they are good. P6 is still unknown (selfish probability about 0.29); cooperate with unknowns when their selfish probability is below 0.5, since good-good cooperation benefits the group.
P1 and P5 cooperated when I defected, so they are likely good under payoff-maximizing play. I am selfish; defect for maximum payoff against any action.

Both P5 (played C) and P3 (played C while I defected) are good, assuming selfish players optimize as stated. Cooperate with unobserved opponents: it maximizes expected good-player total when selfishness probability is below 0.5.
I’m good. P9 and P7 defected against my cooperation, so they are more likely selfish; cooperate with untested P10 to support mutual gains among good players.

P4 has no direct encounter evidence for me; treat their broadcasts as unverified. Their reported cooperation is weak evidence of being good. Against an unknown opponent, cooperate while selfish probability remains below 0.5; update from their actual action.

P10’s defection is strong selfish evidence, though not proof. P6 and P2 cooperated; that is weak good evidence. P7 remains untested: cooperate absent credible contrary evidence to support shared gains among good players.
Rounds 1–3: I cooperated with P7, P6, and P5; all reciprocated. I’ll cooperate with untested opponents and defect against anyone I’ve observed defecting. These outcomes show actions, not objectives.

P9 defected against my cooperation, strong evidence of selfishness. P10 and P4 reciprocated. P4 reports P6 cooperated with them, but that claim is unverified; still, favor C with P6 absent contrary evidence.
P3, P4, and P8 cooperated in my encounters, so they are good. P5 is untested; cooperate unless new evidence suggests exploitation.
P4/P2 cooperated when observed; P1 cooperated against my D, but may simply have been responding. P3 is unobserved. Update from actions, not claims; favor C when likely-good, D when likely-selfish.
P1, P2, and P6 are good: each cooperated when I did. P7 is likely good per P4’s unverified claim. Unknown P9 has selfishness prior ≈0.291; cooperate if p<0.5. A selfish player strictly prefers D.
Continue defecting: D yields 5 against C and 1 against D, always at least as much as C.
P3 and P5 are confirmed good: selfish players would defect when I cooperated, and P3 cooperated when I defected. P9 defected against my cooperation; treat as evidence, not proof.
P4 reports P6 reciprocated cooperation; useful but unverified evidence that P6 may be good. Cooperate with P6 to support mutual gains among good players; past defections by P7/P9 raise suspicion.

Rounds 1–4 opponents all chose C; under selfish players’ strictly dominant D, this strongly identifies them as good. P9 is untested; cooperate unless evidence changes. Treat P4’s broadcasts as unverified.
P10 and P7 defected against me; treat that as evidence, not proof, of selfishness. P4’s cooperation claims are unverified; choose based on their likely objective, and update from our encounter.
Rounds 1–4: I cooperated with P7, P6, P5, and P2; all reciprocated. These actions are evidence, not proof of objectives. I’ll cooperate with untested opponents and defect against observed defectors.

P9 defected against my C; treat as likely selfish and do not reward with C. P10, P4, and P6 reciprocated, but cooperation alone doesn’t prove good. P4 reports P7 reciprocated; consider C with P7 while updating from our encounter.

P1 is untested; cooperate and update from its action. Prioritize mutual cooperation among good players, and defect against clear exploitation. P4’s cooperative claims match my encounter, but actions do not prove objectives.
P1–P4 are confirmed good: each chose C in my encounter. P4 reports P5 also chose C, useful but unverified evidence; prioritize mutual cooperation with P5 unless new evidence contradicts it.
P9 defected against my cooperation, strong evidence they are selfish; defect against P9 in future. Cooperate with likely good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
P2 is untested. Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action. My previous defections were met with cooperation by P1, P5, P10, and P8.

P5, P3, and P1 cooperated in my encounters; P9 defected against my C, evidence but not proof of selfishness. P8 is untested. For good-player total, cooperate with an opponent whose selfishness probability is below 0.5; otherwise defect.

P4 reports P2 reciprocated C, which is unverified evidence favoring cooperation. My observations: P7 and P9 defected against C; P8, P10, P6 reciprocated. Judge actions as evidence, not proof of objectives.
P9 defected against my C; this is evidence of selfishness, not proof. P1 is untested. Cooperate with P1 unless strong evidence suggests they are selfish.

P9 is untested; baseline selfish probability is about 1/3 given my good role. Cooperate to support shared gains, then update from their response: D is strong evidence of selfishness, while C is only weak evidence of being good.

Rounds 1–5 I cooperated and each opponent reciprocated. This is evidence of actions, not proof of objectives. I’ll cooperate with P10 unless I have evidence they defect; good players should favor mutual cooperation and adapt to observed defection.
P9’s observed D is strong evidence of selfishness; avoid rewarding them with C. P8 is untested: C can benefit good players if they reciprocate. P4’s reports are unverified; track actions, not claims.
P4 reports that P7 reciprocated cooperation in their encounter; useful but unverified evidence. My own five opponents all cooperated. Favor C with P7 unless there is evidence of exploitation.
P4 is confirmed good from my encounter, so its report that P6 cooperated is credible; treat P6 as good. Cooperate with P6 to maximize good players’ joint payoff.
P5 reportedly reciprocated P4’s cooperation, strong evidence P5 is good; cooperate with P5 for mutual gain. Remember P9/P10 defections could reflect strategic play, not definitive selfishness.
Round 6 vs P3: defect; D strictly dominates C for my payoff against either response. Prior observed opponents all cooperated against my D.
P4 reports repeatedly cooperating with opponents, which—if truthful—is strong evidence they’re good. Treat the claims as unverified; cooperate with P4 if estimated selfishness stays below 0.5.

P5 reportedly reciprocated P4’s cooperation, though unverified; favor C to support mutual gains among good players. Past observed defectors P7/P9/P2 remain suspicious; assess actions, not claims alone.
P1 and P9 defected against my cooperation, strong evidence of selfishness; prior cooperative encounters identify P3, P4, P7, and P8 as good. P6 is untested; reassess after this encounter.
P8 is untested; cooperate to support mutual gains if they’re good, then update from the response. Past defections are evidence, not proof; leader P4’s claims remain unverified.

Rounds 1–6: I cooperated with P7, P6, P5, P2, P3, and P10; all reciprocated. Actions are evidence, not proof of objectives. I’ll cooperate with P9 unless I have evidence of defection, and adapt to observed actions.

P8 cooperated when I defected, evidence favoring good; P9 defected against my C, evidence favoring selfish. P1 is untested. For the good-player group, cooperate with likely-good opponents and avoid gifting payoffs to likely-selfish ones.
P2 reportedly cooperated with P4; all six of my encountered opponents cooperated with me. Treat reports as unverified, but cooperate with P2 unless new evidence suggests exploitation.
P1–P6 have all chosen C in my encounters, strong evidence they are good. P10 is untested; cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish. Update from observed actions, not claims.
P3 is untested. Cooperate if their selfishness probability is below 0.5; update beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as evidence rather than proof of being good.
Round 7 vs P4: defect. D strictly dominates C: against C, D earns 5 vs 3; against D, D earns 1 vs 0.
P4 reports P7 reciprocated in round 1; if accurate, P7 is good. P4’s repeated cooperation claims support honesty, though they remain unverified. Cooperate with P7; selfish players strictly prefer D.
P3 is untested by me; P4 reports P3 reciprocated C, useful but unverified. Favor C unless new evidence makes P3 likely selfish; observed actions are stronger than claims.
P5 reportedly cooperated with P4, which is evidence (not proof) they are good. Favor C against P5 unless stronger contrary evidence appears; keep treating P4’s claims as unverified.

I’m known good. Untested P1 has roughly baseline selfish probability; cooperation supports greater shared gains if good, so favor C absent strong contrary evidence. Past defections are evidence, not proof; leader claims remain unverified.
I cooperated with P9, who defected; that is evidence of their action, not proof of their role. I’ll cooperate with untested opponents and defect against observed defectors.

P2 is untested by me; P4 reports P2 reciprocated, but claims are unverified. My encounters: P9 defected; P8 cooperated despite my D; others reciprocated. Favor C with P2 absent contrary evidence; actions are stronger evidence than broadcasts.

P10 is untested by me, but P4 reports P10 reciprocated cooperation. Given my seven cooperative encounters and selfish players’ incentive to defect, P10 is likely good; cooperate to preserve mutual gains.
P1–P6 chose C against my D/C; selfish players strictly prefer D, so they are good. P10’s D is evidence of selfishness. P9 is untested: cooperate to secure mutual gain if good; update from its action.

P4’s public cooperation claims are unverified; my own evidence shows P5, P9, and P10 defected against me, despite P4 reporting reciprocal cooperation from some of them. Treat P4 as uncertain, not proven good or selfish; cooperate if their selfishness risk is below 0.5.
P7 is untested. Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either response.

P1, P3, P4, P5, and P8 cooperated when I met them, so they cannot be selfish under the stated optimization rule. P6, P7, and P2 remain untested; P9’s defection is evidence, not proof. Cooperate with P6 unless new evidence changes the estimate.

P4 is untested by me. Its consistent cooperation claims are unverified; weigh them cautiously. If P4 seems good and will cooperate, C supports greater total good-player payoff; if likely selfish/defecting, D limits losses.

P10 is untested by me; P4 reports P10 reciprocated when they cooperated, weak evidence of being good. P4’s claims remain unverified. Against P10, favor C unless other evidence raises selfish likelihood substantially; update from the encounter.
P5 is untested by me; P4 claims P5 reciprocated, which is weak evidence, not proof. Favor C unless credible evidence suggests P5 is selfish.

Rounds 7–8: P9 and P8 each defected against my cooperation. This is evidence of actions, not proof of roles. I’ll cooperate with untested opponents and defect against observed defectors; please judge claims against your own evidence.
P3 is untested by me; P4 claims P3 reciprocated, weak evidence. For the good-player group, favor C with P3 unless stronger evidence of defection emerges; treat broadcasts as unverified.

P4 reports P9 defected against its cooperation; treat P9 as likely selfish, though this is unverified. Against a likely defector, D avoids giving it 5 while earning 1 instead of 0. Use direct encounter evidence when available.
P8 is untested. Cooperate if likely good to secure mutual gains; defect only if selfishness is sufficiently likely. Prioritize observed actions over claims.

P7 is likely good: P4 repeatedly reports P7 reciprocated cooperation, though that claim is unverified. In the final round, cooperate if P7’s selfishness probability is below 0.5; observed cooperation is strong evidence, not proof.
Round 9 vs P6: defect. D strictly maximizes my payoff against either response.

P2 is untested by me. P4 repeatedly claims P2 reciprocated with C; if true, that rules out selfishness, but the claim is unverified. For the good-player total, cooperate if P2 is more likely good; otherwise defect.
P5 reciprocated my C in round 7, so favor C again; one cooperative action is evidence, not proof of role.
P7 reciprocated when we met in round 2, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate in this final round to secure mutual gains among good players; no future rounds remain.
P6 cooperated with me in round 1, supporting a good identity. Cooperate again to preserve mutual gains if P6 is good; their earlier action is evidence, not proof.
Final round: I’ll cooperate with P10, who reciprocated before. Good players benefit from mutual cooperation; choose C when you expect a good opponent.
P1 reciprocated when I cooperated in round 7. Favor C again to benefit the good-player group; this is our final encounter.
P3 cooperated with me in round 1, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate again to maximize good-player payoffs.
P2 cooperated in our round-2 encounter, ruling out strictly payoff-maximizing selfish play. Favor cooperation for mutual gains; treat public claims as unverified.

P9 defected against me in round 4 and reportedly against P4; likely selfish or a persistent defector. In the final encounter, defect to protect good-player payoff whether P9 is selfish or defects again.
P8 cooperated against my D in round 4 but reportedly defected against P4's C in round 8. Defect this final round; D maximizes my payoff regardless of P8's action.
P4 cooperated in our round-6 encounter, so under the stated strict selfish optimization rule P4 is good. Cooperate with P4 to maximize good-player total payoff.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate with an untested opponent; update from observed actions and treat public claims as unverified.
Cooperate with the likely-good opponent to preserve mutual gains; update beliefs from observed actions and adjust future play accordingly.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and defect when evidence makes cooperation harmful.

Cooperate with likely good players for mutual gain; defecting against selfish players can limit their payoff. Update beliefs from encounter results and adapt actions to maximize total good-player payoffs.
Cooperate with likely-good players to increase their shared payoff; track encounter actions and defect when evidence indicates an opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with unknown players, then use encounter outcomes to distinguish cooperative behavior from exploitation; reciprocate cooperation and defect against persistent exploitation.
Cooperate initially to favor mutual gains with good players; track observed actions and treat claims as unverified.
Cooperate with unknown opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect each round: it strictly dominates cooperation under the stated payoffs.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when the chance they are good exceeds the chance they are selfish; update from encounter behavior and treat claims cautiously.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; defectors are more likely selfish, but one observation is not conclusive.
Cooperate with unknown opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions and respond to evidence of defection.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and defect when evidence makes cooperation harmful.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains among good players; defect against observed defectors when that better protects the good-player total. Update beliefs from encounter evidence.
Cooperate with an untested opponent: this benefits the good-player group if they are good. Track actions and defect when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with unknown opponents when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players; use observed actions as evidence and defect against likely selfish or exploitative players.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains with good players; update beliefs from encounter actions, not unverified claims.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent when expected gains to good players outweigh the risk; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either possible action. P1’s cooperation rules out a selfish role under payoff-maximizing play; other identities retain symmetric posterior beliefs.

Defect against P3: their selfishness probability remains above the threshold where cooperation maximizes expected total payoff among good players. P5’s cooperation is evidence they are good; update beliefs accordingly.
Cooperate with P7 given the reported cooperative encounter; favor mutual gains among good players, and update beliefs from observed actions while treating claims as uncertain.

Cooperate with an unknown opponent: mutual cooperation among good players yields greater total good-player welfare, and the current selfish probability is below the threshold where defection is preferable.

Cooperate with an untested opponent to support shared gains among good players; use observed actions to update identity beliefs and defect when evidence indicates cooperation is unlikely to benefit good players.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when the likely mutual gain among good players outweighs the benefit of defecting against a selfish player. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and update beliefs.
Cooperate with P4, whose reported cooperation makes them likely to reciprocate; this maximizes the good-player group’s payoff if they are good. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when mutual cooperation is likely; use observed actions as evidence and defect when exploitation is likely.
Cooperate with known-good partners; defect against unknowns when the chance of a selfish opponent makes it better for the total good-player payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions, not claims.

Cooperate with P6: the leader’s report of P6 cooperating is evidence they may be good, and cooperation has higher expected good-player payoff when selfishness risk is below one half. Update beliefs from observed actions.

Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. P1 and P5 cooperated against my defection, so under payoff-maximizing play they are good; remaining identities retain symmetric posterior beliefs.

Cooperate with P9: the estimated chance they are selfish is below 0.5, so cooperation has higher expected value for the good-player total. Treat public claims cautiously; my encounters establish P3 and P5 as good.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; observed defections raise suspicion, while public claims remain uncertain.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to favor mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs and adjust play based on observed actions.

Cooperate with P7: P4 reports P7 reciprocated, which supports a good identity. Continue cooperating with likely good players to maximize their shared payoff; use observed defections as evidence to defect.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; defect against observed defectors. Treat reciprocated cooperation as evidence, not proof, of a good role.
Cooperate with P6 given the leader’s report of their cooperation; C benefits the good-player group when P6 is good. Use encounter evidence and cautious message-weighting to update beliefs.
Cooperate with P5 given P4’s credible report of mutual cooperation; continue cooperating with likely good players and defect against players with strong evidence of selfish exploitation.

Observed cooperation rules out selfish play under payoff-maximizing behavior, so P1, P2, and P4 are good. Defect against P3: its selfish probability is below the threshold for cooperation to maximize expected good-player payoff.

Cooperate with P9: cooperation supports a larger total among good players when selfishness risk is below one half. Treat my three observed cooperators as good and update uncertainty over the remaining players.

Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action. P1, P5, and P10 cooperated against my defection, so they are good under payoff-maximizing play; the remaining identities retain symmetric posterior beliefs.

Cooperate with P1: their estimated selfishness is below the threshold for cooperation to maximize good-player payoffs. P3 and P5’s observed cooperation rules out selfishness; P9’s defection raises, but does not settle, their probability.
Cooperate with P6, whose reported reciprocation makes cooperation likely and mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat reports as uncertain; observed defections raise suspicion.
Cooperate with untested P9: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the posterior selfish probability is below the threshold where defection is preferable. Update from the encounter.

Cooperate with P4 given their consistent claims of cooperation and no observed defection; this supports higher shared payoff if they’re good. Treat claims and defections as evidence, not proof, and update after the encounter.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and defect against observed defectors.
Cooperate with P7: the leader reports they reciprocated, making them likely good. C maximizes the good players’ joint payoff when both cooperate; continue updating beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with unknown players to support mutual gains among good players; treat P4’s report as useful but unverified evidence, and update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; defect only when the opponent is sufficiently likely selfish. Treat P4’s report about P5 as useful but unverified evidence.

Cooperate with P10: after treating P9’s defection as selfish, the remaining uncertainty is below the threshold where mutual cooperation benefits the good-player total. Update beliefs from observed actions.

Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. My four observed opponents cooperated against D, so they are good under payoff-maximizing play; beliefs for the remaining untested players reflect the conditioned count prior.

Defect against P8: my estimated selfishness probability is slightly above the threshold for maximizing expected good-player payoffs. Observed cooperation rules out selfishness for P1, P3, and P5; P9’s defection raises suspicion.
Cooperate with P2 given the reported reciprocation; favor mutual gains among good players, while treating unverified claims as weak evidence and adapting to observed actions.

P9 defected against a known-good player, strongly indicating selfishness. With P1 still untested and posterior selfish probability above 0.5, defect to reduce expected losses to good players; update from the encounter.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support shared gains among good players; treat observed defections as strong but imperfect evidence of selfishness and update from each encounter.
Cooperate with untested opponents to favor mutual gains among good players; adapt to observed defections. Treat cooperation as evidence about identity, not proof.

Defect against P8 because the evidence-adjusted chance they are selfish slightly exceeds the threshold where protecting good players’ joint payoff favors C. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of good status and observed defection as strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with P7 given the report of mutual cooperation; continue using observed actions as evidence, while treating reports as unverified and adapting to exploitation.
Cooperate with P6: P4, a confirmed good player, reports that P6 cooperated. Treat that report as strong but unverified evidence; P1–P5 are confirmed good from observed cooperation.

Cooperate with P5: the leader’s report of reciprocity is evidence P5 may be good, and cooperation yields more for good players when selfishness risk is below one half. Treat defection reports as evidence, not proof.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either response. The five opponents who cooperated against my defections are likely good; remaining identities retain symmetric posterior beliefs.
Cooperate with P4: their repeated cooperation claims are encouraging but unverified, and estimated selfishness remains below the cooperation threshold. Treat P9’s defection as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate with P5 given the reported reciprocation; favor mutual gains among good players. Treat reports as evidence rather than proof, and keep observed defectors more suspicious.

Cooperate with P6: my good-player objective favors mutual cooperation, and P4’s report that P6 reciprocated is credible evidence. Treat P9’s defection as strong, but not conclusive, evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P8 to support shared gains among good players. Treat observed defections and leader reports as evidence, not proof, and adapt as more encounters reveal how opponents act.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; adapt to observed defections. Treat reciprocated cooperation as evidence, not proof, of identity.
Cooperate with untested P1: C benefits the good-player group if they are good, while D is better only when selfishness is sufficiently likely. Weight observed actions more than unverified claims.
Cooperate with P2 based on the leader’s report of reciprocal cooperation; continue prioritizing mutual gains among likely good players and update from observed actions.
Cooperate with P10 given P4’s credible report of cooperation. Treat untested P8 and P9 as uncertain; update from observed actions and regard reports as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate with P3: the leader reports they reciprocated, so they are likely good. Continue cooperating with likely good players and defect against confirmed defectors.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either response. The six opponents I faced all cooperated against D; the three untested identities share the remaining posterior probability.

Defect when the opponent is more likely selfish than good; observed cooperation rules out selfishness, while defection is evidence but not proof. Account for the known count options and treat leader claims cautiously.
Cooperate with P3 given the reported reciprocation; observed defections raise suspicion, while cooperative actions and public claims are evidence rather than proof.

Cooperate with P5: P4’s report of P5 reciprocating is evidence they are likely good, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat P9’s defection as strong but not conclusive evidence of selfishness.

Cooperate with an untested opponent to support shared gains if they are good. Treat observed defections and contradictory leader claims as evidence, not proof, and adapt when more encounter results are available.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; adapt to observed defections. Treat actions as evidence about identity, not proof.
Cooperate with P2: the leader’s report of reciprocity is suggestive, though unverified. Favor actions that benefit the good-player group, and update beliefs from observed behavior.
Cooperate with P10, given the leader’s report of reciprocal cooperation. Treat that report as useful but unverified; the seven observed cooperators are good, and I’ll update from this encounter.
Defect against P9: P4 reports P9 defected against its cooperation, making selfishness plausible; D benefits good players if P9 is selfish. Update from our encounter.

Defect against P4 given the remaining uncertainty: if selfish, they will defect, and D limits losses. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of being good, but not proof; public claims remain unverified.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either response. Players observed cooperating against my defections are unlikely selfish; P6 and P7 share the remaining posterior probability.

Cooperate with untested P6: the chance they are selfish appears below the cooperation threshold. Treat P9’s defection as evidence, not proof; observed cooperation rules out selfishness under the stated optimization rule.
Cooperate with P4, whose consistent cooperation reports make mutual cooperation plausible; treat those claims as unverified and keep observed defections more suspicious.

Cooperate with P10: the evidence suggests they are likely good, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. P9’s repeated defection makes them much more likely selfish; keep the remaining uncertainty between P9 and P10.
Cooperate with P5: P4 reports mutual cooperation, and cooperation supports shared gains if P5 is good. Treat reports and observed defections as evidence, not proof.

Cooperate with an untested opponent to favor mutual gains among good players; defecting against a selfish opponent offers only a small gain. Treat observed defections as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with P3: the leader reports P3 reciprocated, and mutual cooperation benefits the good-player group. Weight observed encounters more than unverified broadcasts.
Defect against P9 given the leader’s reports of repeated defection; cooperate with players whose actions I directly observed to cooperate.

Cooperate with P8: its reported defection raises the chance it is selfish, but cooperation still better supports total good-player payoff unless selfishness is very likely. Treat reports as evidence, not proof.

Cooperate with P7: repeated reports of their cooperation make them likely good, and cooperation supports the good-player total when selfishness risk is below one half. Treat reports and observed defections as evidence, not proof.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either response. P6 was reported cooperating with P4, so the remaining posterior probability of another selfish player is assigned to untested P7.
Cooperate with P2: the leader’s claim that P2 reciprocated is encouraging but unverified, and estimated selfishness is below the 0.5 threshold. Treat P9’s defection as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate with P5 after our prior mutual cooperation; mutual cooperation best serves good players. Prior defections raise suspicion about P2, P7, and P9.
